Measure the screener against a hand-screened sample

Source: R/doc-screen-calibrate.R
gr_calibrate.Rd

Compares gr_screen()'s decisions with a person's on the same documents, and reports what that sample supports: how much of the eligible literature the screener kept, how much of the irrelevant literature it removed, and how much reading it saved. Each comes with an interval, and each is refused when the sample is too small to say.

Usage

gr_calibrate(
  screening,
  reference,
  positive = "include",
  min_positives = 10L,
  of = NULL,
  recall_target = 0.95,
  conf = 0.95,
  max_lost = NULL
)

Arguments

screening

A gr_screening from gr_screen(), or a data frame shaped like its $table, for instance read back from a CSV. Its decision must be "include", "exclude", "unclear" or empty (never read), in any case; a row whose status says it was not read counts as never read.

reference

The completed frame from gr_reference(), a path to the filled-in CSV, or any data frame with document and human_decision (or one human_decision_<reviewer> column per reviewer; see "Several reviewers").

positive

Which human decision counts as eligible: "include" or "exclude".

min_positives

For an "all" sample: below this many eligible studies the sensitivity estimate is reported but marked inadequate. A sample of one stratum is judged by its interval instead; see "What a small sample cannot do".

of

Which part of the screening run the reference was drawn from: "excluded", "kept", "all" or "stacked"; anything else is an error. "stacked" also reads a kept sheet and an excluded sheet stacked with rbind() as one stratified reference. Normally recovered from the file gr_reference() wrote; give it explicitly for a reference built by hand. Given over a file that records a different frame, it wins with a warning, and the file's frame size is not used.

recall_target

The recall the screener should reach, strictly between 0 and 1.

conf

Confidence level of the recall and loss bounds.

max_lost

Optional: the most eligible records the screener may have excluded. When given, an upper bound on records lost at or below it also meets the target.

Value

An object of class gr_calibration:

counts

The confusion matrix, as kept/excluded by eligible/not.

metrics

One row per statistic: estimate, lower, upper, n.

kappa

Cohen's kappa on kept against excluded; NA for a sample of one stratum.

agreement

kept (the primary table) and strict (include against the rest), each a list of table, n, stats (one row per statistic: statistic, estimate, lower, upper) and paradox. NULL for a sample of one stratum.

kappa_legacy

Deprecated: the 0.6.0 kappa on the screener's three labels against the person's two. Removed in the next release.

decisions

The 3x2 counts: the screener's include, unclear and exclude by the person's eligible and not.

missed

The eligible studies the screener excluded: the rows themselves, because a list of the misses says more than a rate.

disagreements

Every row where the two differ, in either direction.

adequate

Whether the sample supports a claim from its frame's headline rate: sensitivity in an "all" sample, the frame's own rate in an "excluded" or "kept" one.

adequacy

How that was judged: rule ("positives", "interval" or "whole frame"), bar, width, and note, a sentence saying why the sample fell short (NA when it did not).

frame

Which rows the sample was drawn from, and how many.

recall

Recall: estimate, lower and upper (two-sided at conf), bound (the one-sided lower bound), method, conf, n (eligible records in the sample) and note. NA where the frame cannot estimate it.

lost

M, the projected number of eligible records excluded: estimate, lower, upper, bound (the one-sided upper bound), frame_n (records excluded) and conf.

false_exclusion

The share of excluded records that are eligible: estimate, lower, upper (exact) and n.

work_saved

The share of screened records the screener excluded, which nobody reads: estimate, excluded, screened.

unclear_rate

The share of screened records left unclear: estimate, unclear, screened.

strata

One row per stratum the frame drew from: N, n, eligible, inclusion_prob, and the estimated eligible count with its exact two-sided bounds.

verdict

met (TRUE, FALSE, or NA when nothing bounds recall or M), rule, recall_target, conf, max_lost and note.

reviewers

Only for a sheet with several reviewers: reviewers (their labels), n_reviewers, rule (how the consensus was formed), conflicts (documents they disagreed on), consensus (how each document's consensus was reached, counted), weighted, sensitivity (one row per reviewer and statistic: estimate, lower, upper, n, method), agreement (one row per pair of reviewers, scope and statistic, the scope being the frame, a stratum or "weighted"), notes and conf.

Two sensitivities, and the gap between them

"unclear" is a deferral, not a miss. A record the screener could not settle goes to a person, so it is not lost, and counting it as a failure would punish the screener for the one behaviour that makes it safe.

So two figures are reported. Sensitivity as deployed asks what fraction of the eligible studies survived: kept, whether by "include" or by "unclear". That is the number that matters, because it is the one where a shortfall is permanent. Strict sensitivity asks what fraction were actively included. The gap between them is the reading a person still has to do, and reporting only the first would flatter a screener that defers everything.

Why accuracy is not reported

Inclusion rates run at a few per cent, so a screener that excluded every record would score around 95% accurate and find nothing. Chance-corrected agreement is reported instead, and never as one number.

Agreement, on the decision that matters

The primary agreement table is the one sensitivity uses: kept ("include" or "unclear") against excluded, by the person's eligible against not. An "unclear" on an eligible record is agreement there, since the record was kept. The secondary table is strict: "include" against everything else.

Each table reports Cohen's kappa beside the statistics that say whether it can be read: the prevalence index (PI) and bias index (BI) of Byrt et al. (1993), the prevalence- and bias-adjusted kappa (PABAK, 2 po - 1) and Gwet's AC1, with intervals, and the class-wise sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV. At a few eligible records in a hundred, kappa moves with the marginals as much as with agreement, and can sit near zero where the two raters agree on almost every record; $agreement$kept$paradox is TRUE when abs(PI) is above 0.8, a heuristic threshold that marks such a table. AC1 has the opposite weakness, a value near 1 from records both raters left out, so it is not read alone either.

The kappa interval is a percentile bootstrap that resamples documents, B = 2000, under a fixed seed so the same sample gives the same interval ($agreement$kept$bootstrap holds B and the seed; the session's random stream is left as it was). The AC1 interval uses the variance of Gwet (2008), as the irrCAC package does, with a t quantile on n - 1 degrees of freedom. The PABAK interval is the Wilson interval on the observed agreement, mapped onto the same scale. Where the two raters agree on every record, disagree on every record, or the sample has fewer than 10 records, the kappa and AC1 intervals would be a point or close to one, so they are left empty and $agreement$kept$note says why.

0.6.0 computed kappa on the screener's three labels against the person's two, so every "unclear" counted as a disagreement. That figure is kept as $kappa_legacy for this release only, so a number already quoted can be traced; it is not the screener's agreement with a person.

The rate of "unclear" decisions is the metric "deferred to a person", with its interval, and the 3x2 counts behind both tables are in $decisions.

A decision a person settled with gr_resolve() is not the screener's, so the comparison uses the screener's own decision, from screener_decision, wherever the table has one.

What a small sample cannot do

Sensitivity is estimated from the eligible studies in the sample and from nothing else. Twelve hand-screened records containing two eligible studies estimate it from two observations, and "1.00" from two observations is not a finding. The intervals are Wilson score intervals, which stay sensible at zero and one where the textbook interval collapses to a point, and $adequate says whether there was enough to support a claim at all.

What "enough" means depends on the frame, because what the headline rate rests on does. In an "all" sample it is sensitivity, estimated from the eligible studies alone, so the sample needs min_positives of them. In an "excluded" or "kept" sample the headline rate ("eligible among the excluded", "eligible among those kept") is taken over every row sampled, so a sample of 500 clean exclusions is a good one, not one resting on no observations. There the sample is adequate when that rate's interval is at most 10 percentage points wide, or when every record in the stratum was judged (nothing is left to sample, and the rate is a count for this run). The bar is a floor, not a verdict: 10 points is wide for an omission rate near zero across a large pile of exclusions, and the projected count of lost studies, printed with its interval, is the figure to judge that by. $adequacy$note says in a sentence why a sample fell short.

Recall against a target

Every calibration also reports recall, the share of eligible records the screener kept, against recall_target, with bounds that stay valid at the zero or one misses a reference usually finds.

On a stacked reference (every kept record, and a simple random sample of n of the N excluded ones; of = "stacked") the eligible count is K among the kept and x in the sample, and recall is estimated with the design weights, the ratio of Horvitz-Thompson totals from hr_ht_estimate(): K / (K + M), with M = N x / n the projected number of eligible records excluded. M is bounded exactly from the hypergeometric distribution of x: its upper bound M_U is the largest M for which drawing x or fewer has probability above alpha = 1 - conf, and the lower bound the smallest M for which drawing x or more does. Recall falls as M rises, so its one-sided lower bound is K / (K + M_U). If the kept records were sampled too, each sampled stratum is bounded the same way with alpha split equally between them (Bonferroni). The interval in $recall is two-sided at conf, with alpha / 2 on each side; $recall$bound is the one-sided bound at conf. No bootstrap is used: with x = 0 every resample also gives M = 0, and the interval would be [1, 1].

On a sample of everything screened ("all") the eligible records in the sample are a random sample of all of them, and recall is the share kept with a Clopper-Pearson bound (Lewis, Yang and Frieder 2021). That bound treats the frame as infinite. When the sample is every screened record (gr_reference(n = Inf)) recall is known exactly, and the estimate is also both ends of the interval and the bound (method = "census"). A sample of the exclusions alone bounds M and the false-exclusion rate but not recall, since it does not count the eligible records kept, and a sample of the kept records alone holds none of the misses.

The verdict in $verdict says the target is met when the one-sided lower bound on recall is at least recall_target, or, when max_lost is given, when the upper bound on M is at most max_lost. On a stacked reference this verdict is also $adequate.

Weights come from the run: N is the number of records the screening excluded (or kept), and n the rows of that stratum with a human decision. On a complete sheet that is the inclusion probability the sheet records; a sheet whose recorded probabilities disagree is weighted by the run, with a warning. Agreement statistics are not computed on a stacked reference, since unweighted they are distorted in the same direction as unweighted sensitivity.

One row per document

The reference is matched to the screening by document name, compared as UTF-8 whatever the session's locale, and by document_id for a row whose name still does not match. A document judged twice (two sheets stacked with no reviewer column, say) is counted once when the copies agree, with a warning, and is refused when they disagree.

Several reviewers

A sheet with one human_decision_<reviewer> column per reviewer (from gr_reference(reviewers = k)), or a long sheet with a reviewer column, is compared on the reviewers' consensus. Where it has been formed with gr_reference_consensus() that is used; otherwise records the reviewers agreed on take their decision, records they disagreed on take the consensus column, and the calibration stops if any disagreement has none, saying how many there were.

$reviewers then reports how far the people agree with each other, the yardstick for the screener's agreement with them, with hr_agreement(): for every pair of reviewers the observed agreement, Cohen's kappa, PABAK, Gwet's AC1 and the prevalence and bias indices, never kappa alone, and with three reviewers or more Krippendorff's alpha over all of them. It also reports each reviewer's sensitivity and specificity against the consensus, the share of consensus-eligible records they included and of consensus-ineligible records they excluded, which says what one person screening alone would have missed. A reviewer is scored on the records they judged. Note that a reviewer is part of the consensus they are scored against, so these figures are higher than against an independent reference, and more so with fewer reviewers.

On a stacked reference both are weighted the way recall is, each record by N_h / n_h for its stratum h (the screener's kept or excluded records), so they describe every record screened rather than the sample. Sensitivity is sum_h (N_h / n_h) a_h / sum_h (N_h / n_h) (a_h + b_h), with a_h the consensus-eligible records the reviewer included in stratum h and b_h those they excluded; its interval bounds each count in a sampled stratum exactly with the hypergeometric distribution, alpha split equally over them (Bonferroni), and maps them through the ratio, which rises with a and falls with b. Specificity is the same with the consensus-ineligible records. Agreement is computed on the 2x2 table built with the same weights, with percentile intervals from a bootstrap within each sampled stratum (B = 2000, seed 1), and hr_agreement() is also reported within each stratum. The weighted kappa interval is approximate and runs narrow when the sampled exclusion stratum holds fewer than about 100 records (near 80% coverage for a nominal 95% at 30), and $reviewers$notes says so; the observed agreement, PABAK and AC1 intervals hold up better there. On any other frame the sample is one simple random sample, the figures are unweighted, and sensitivity and specificity have Wilson intervals, as in $metrics.

References

Lewis, D. D., Yang, E. and Frieder, O. (2021). Certifying one-phase technology-assisted reviews. Proceedings of the 30th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management, 893-902.

Horvitz, D. G. and Thompson, D. J. (1952). A generalization of sampling without replacement from a finite universe. Journal of the American Statistical Association 47(260), 663-685.

Byrt, T., Bishop, J. and Carlin, J. B. (1993). Bias, prevalence and kappa. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 46(5), 423-429.

Gwet, K. L. (2008). Computing inter-rater reliability and its variance in the presence of high agreement. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology 61(1), 29-48.

Examples

tab <- data.frame(document = paste0("d", 1:8, ".pdf"),
                  decision = c("include", "include", "unclear", "exclude",
                               "exclude", "exclude", "include", "exclude"),
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
ref <- data.frame(document = paste0("d", 1:8, ".pdf"),
                  human_decision = c("include", "exclude", "include", "exclude",
                                     "exclude", "include", "include", "exclude"),
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gr_calibrate(structure(list(table = tab), class = "gr_screening"), ref)
#> Warning: This reference does not say which part of the screening run it came from, so the figures below assume a sample of EVERYTHING screened. If it is a sample of one stratum (the exclusions, say), sensitivity and specificity are artifacts of that frame rather than facts about the screener. Pass `of = "excluded"`, `"kept"` or `"all"` to say which.
#> <gr_calibration> 8 hand-screened row(s), 4 eligible
#>   sampled from: unknown (NA of 8 screened)
#>   sensitivity (as deployed)       75.0%  [30.1%, 95.4%]  n=4
#>   sensitivity (strict include)    50.0%  [15.0%, 85.0%]  n=4
#>   specificity                     75.0%  [30.1%, 95.4%]  n=4
#>   deferred to a person            12.5%  [2.2%, 47.1%]  n=8
#>   reading avoided                 50.0%  [21.5%, 78.5%]  n=8
#>   screener    eligible  not eligible
#>   include            2             1
#>   unclear            1             0
#>   exclude            1             3
#>   agreement, kept (include + unclear) vs excluded:
#>     kappa     0.50  [--, --]
#>     PABAK     0.50  [-0.18, 0.86]
#>     AC1       0.50  [--, --]
#>     PI 0.00, BI 0.00
#>     (no kappa or AC1 interval: Only 8 record(s); the kappa and AC1 intervals need at least 10.)
#>   agreement, strict include vs the rest:
#>     kappa     0.25  [--, --]
#>     PABAK     0.25  [-0.39, 0.73]
#>     AC1       0.26  [--, --]
#>     PI -0.12, BI -0.12
#>     (no kappa or AC1 interval: Only 8 record(s); the kappa and AC1 intervals need at least 10.)
#>   recall 75.0%  [75.0%, 75.0%]; 95% one-sided lower bound 75.0%
#>   eligible records excluded: about 1 of 4; 95% upper bound 1
#>   recall target 95.0% at 95% confidence: not met
#>   ! 1 eligible study was excluded by the screener:
#>       d6.pdf
#>   ! only 4 eligible studies in the sample. Every rate above rests on
#>     those 4 observations, which is why the intervals are as wide as they are.
